title: Matthew, the Gospel and the Evangelist
lead: Matthew, one of the Twelve, called from a tax booth in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9), to whom the church from the 100s on credited the first Gospel. The Gospel itself names no author; many scholars think it was written by an unknown Jewish-Christian teacher after AD 70.

sections.b: Matthew 9:9 tells of a tax collector named Matthew whom Jesus called; Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 tell the same story of "Levi son of Alphaeus." Matthew 10:3 calls him "Matthew the tax collector" in the list of the Twelve. Whether Matthew and Levi were one man with two names, like Simon Peter, is debated. Nothing else certain is known of him; later traditions send him to Ethiopia, Parthia or Persia.
sections.refs: Matthew 9:9; Matthew 10:3; Mark 2:14; Mark 3:18; Luke 5:27; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13

sections.b: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis (about AD 110–130), as quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.39.16), wrote that "Matthew put the sayings (logia) in order in the Hebrew dialect, and each person translated them as he was able." Irenaeus (about 180) said Matthew wrote a Gospel "among the Hebrews in their own language." From then on the church named Matthew as author. Many modern scholars doubt this, because our Greek Matthew does not read like a translation and seems to use Mark's Greek, which an eyewitness would hardly need. They suggest an anonymous Jewish-Christian teacher, perhaps one of the scribes Jesus describes in Matthew 13:52, "every scribe who has become a disciple for the kingdom of heaven". Others (for example R. T. France, Craig Keener, and earlier Catholic tradition) still hold that the apostle stands behind the Gospel in some way.
